claim: Magnetothermal genetic stimulation provides tetherless deep brain activation sufficient to evoke motor behavior in awake mice.
source: Here, we demonstrate that magnetothermal genetic stimulation provides tetherless deep brain activation sufficient to evoke motor behavior in awake mice.
evidence: This is the main finding stated in the abstract, supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript showing behavioral responses in mice.

claim: The approach uses alternating magnetic fields to heat superparamagnetic nanoparticles on the neuronal membrane.
source: The approach uses alternating magnetic fields to heat superparamagnetic nanoparticles on the neuronal membrane.
evidence: This describes the mechanism of the technique, which is demonstrated experimentally in the manuscript.

claim: Neurons heat-sensitized by expressing TRPV1 are activated with magnetic field application.
source: Neurons, heat-sensitized by expressing TRPV1 are activated with magnetic field application.
evidence: This is demonstrated through in vitro calcium imaging experiments showing neuronal activation.

claim: Magnetothermal genetic stimulation in the motor cortex evoked ambulation.
source: Magnetothermal genetic stimulation in the motor cortex evoked ambulation
evidence: This is supported by behavioral tracking data showing increased locomotion during AMF application in motor cortex-injected mice.

claim: Deep brain stimulation in the striatum caused rotation around the body-axis.
source: deep brain stimulation in the striatum caused rotation around the body-axis
evidence: This is demonstrated by behavioral tracking showing rotational behavior in striatum-injected mice during AMF application.

claim: Stimulation near the ridge between ventral and dorsal striatum caused freezing-of-gait.
source: stimulation near the ridge between ventral and dorsal striatum caused freezing-of-gait.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data showing immobilization of limbs during AMF application in deep striatum-injected mice.

claim: The duration of the behavior correlated tightly with field application.
source: The duration of the behavior correlated tightly with field application.
evidence: This is demonstrated by temporal tracking data showing behavior onset and offset corresponding to AMF on and off times.

claim: This approach provides genetically and spatially targetable, repeatable and temporarily precise activation of deep-brain circuits without the need for surgical implantation of any device.
source: This approach provides genetically and spatially targetable, repeatable and temporarily precise activation of deep-brain circuits without the need for surgical implantation of any device.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental design using viral gene delivery and nanoparticle injection without permanent implants, and repeated successful stimulations.

claim: Optogenetics requires permanent brain implants to guide the light into the brain, and typically, an optical fiber, tethering the animal to the light source.
source: However, optogenetics requires permanent brain implants to guide the light into the brain, and typically, an optical fiber, tethering the animal to the light source.
evidence: This is established knowledge about optogenetic techniques.

claim: Optogenetics has been used in various animal models to study brain circuits associated with Parkinson's Disease.
source: The method quickly gained popularity and has been used in various animal models to study brain circuits associated with Parkinson's Disease (Gradinaru et al., 2009; Kravitz et al., 2010)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Optogenetics has been used to study addictive behavior.
source: The method quickly gained popularity and has been used in various animal models to study brain circuits associated with Parkinson's Disease (Gradinaru et al., 2009; Kravitz et al., 2010), addictive behavior (Chen et al., 2013; Stefanik et al., 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Optogenetics has been used to study depression.
source: The method quickly gained popularity and has been used in various animal models to study brain circuits associated with Parkinson's Disease (Gradinaru et al., 2009; Kravitz et al., 2010), addictive behavior (Chen et al., 2013; Stefanik et al., 2013), depression (Nieh et al., 2013; Zhu et al., 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Optogenetics has been used to study anxiety.
source: The method quickly gained popularity and has been used in various animal models to study brain circuits associated with Parkinson's Disease (Gradinaru et al., 2009; Kravitz et al., 2010), addictive behavior (Chen et al., 2013; Stefanik et al., 2013), depression (Nieh et al., 2013; Zhu et al., 2016) and anxiety (Tye et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: Pharmacological neuromodulation using DREADDs generates a much slower response, ranging from tens of minutes to hours, as the drug must diffuse to the location of action.
source: A third approach, pharmacological neuromodulation using Designer GPCRs Exclusively Activated by Designer Drugs (DREADDs), provides a tetherless alternative to optogenetics, but generates a much slower response, ranging from tens of minutes to hours, as the drug must diffuse to the location of action (Armbruster et al., 2007; Urban and Roth, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work on DREADDs.

claim: Magnetic fields are minimally scattered, minimally absorbed by tissue, and travel freely through space.
source: Magnetic-field-based stimulation has considerable potential to provide fast, tetherless, and implant-free deep brain stimulation because magnetic fields are minimally scattered, minimally absorbed by tissue, and travel freely through space (Walsh and Cowey, 2000).
evidence: This is established knowledge about magnetic field properties, supported by citation.

claim: The absence of tethers will permit novel social behavioral assays in a group of animals freely interacting in an arena, while only a subgroup of them gets stimulated.
source: The absence of tethers will permit novel social behavioral assays in a group of animals freely interacting in an arena, while only a subgroup of them gets stimulated.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about potential future applications of the technique.

claim: The absence of any physical connection from brain to skull minimizes tissue damage and immune response.
source: Furthermore, the absence of any physical connection from brain to skull minimizes tissue damage and immune response (Chen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: In very small particles made from materials that are ferromagnetic in bulk, the spins interact, but at room temperature the direction of their magnetic moment relative to the particle fluctuates rapidly.
source: In very small particles made from materials that are ferromagnetic in bulk, the spins interact, but at room temperature the direction of their magnetic moment relative to the particle fluctuates rapidly (Brown, 1963).
evidence: This is established knowledge about superparamagnetic particles, supported by citation.

claim: Superparamagnetic particles are the preferred transducers for magnetic biostimulation.
source: Such particles are called superparamagnetic (Bean and Livingston, 1959). They are the preferred transducers for magnetic biostimulation (Xu and Sun, 2013; Pankhurst et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Applying an alternating magnetic field to superparamagnetic nanoparticles may be used to locally generate heat, which then actives nearby temperature-sensitive TRPV1 channels.
source: Alternatively, our group showed that applying an alternating magnetic field (AMF) to superparamagnetic nanoparticles may be used to locally generate heat, which then actives nearby temperature-sensitive TRPV1 channels (Huang et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work by the authors' group.

claim: For horse ferritin the magnetic dipole at 0.1 T per particle is so weak that the dipole interaction energy is a lot smaller than the thermal energy even if the ferritin molecules were touching each other.
source: However, for horse ferritin the magnetic dipole at 0.1 T per particle is so weak that the dipole interaction energy is a lot smaller than the thermal energy even if the ferritin molecules were touching each other (García-Prieto et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2015a) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by theoretical calculations and citations, with data shown in supplementary figure.

claim: The synthesized nanoparticles used in this study heat by 450 W/g at 500 kHz and 15 kA/m.
source: The synthesized nanoparticles used in this study, heat by 450 W/g at 500 kHz and 15 kA/m, while horse ferritin does not heat in the same AMF (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: Horse ferritin does not heat in an AMF of 500 kHz and 15 kA/m.
source: The synthesized nanoparticles used in this study, heat by 450 W/g at 500 kHz and 15 kA/m, while horse ferritin does not heat in the same AMF (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: Even if increasing the frequency driving ferritin to 50 MHz and 0.15 kA/m horse ferritin heats less than 1 W/g.
source: Even if increasing the frequency driving ferritin to 50 MHz and 0.15 kA/m horse ferritin heats less than 1 W/g.
evidence: This is based on theoretical calculations shown in supplementary figure.

claim: In a two-dimensional dense array of MNPs on the membrane, the neighboring MNPs screen the lateral cooling, leaving only the direction normal to the membrane for heat dissipation.
source: In a two-dimensional dense array of MNPs on the membrane, the neighboring MNPs screen the lateral cooling, leaving only the direction normal to the membrane for heat dissipation.
evidence: This is based on theoretical understanding of heat dissipation from prior work.

claim: Membrane-bound MNPs deliver sufficient power to raise the temperature in a thin sheet along the membrane.
source: Membrane-bound MNPs deliver sufficient power to raise the temperature in a thin sheet along the membrane (Huang et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: This is the first robust and repeated magnetothermal genetic activation of motor behavior in awake, freely moving mice using magnetic nanoparticles.
source: Here, we report the first robust and repeated magnetothermal genetic activation of motor behavior in awake, freely moving mice using magnetic nanoparticles (MNPs), attached to the plasma membrane of temperature-sensitized TRPV1+ neurons, deep inside the brain.
evidence: This is the main claim of the paper, supported by the experimental data presented.

claim: Magnetothermal activation was demonstrated in three separate brain regions: motor cortex, dorsal striatum and the ridge between dorsal and ventral striatum.
source: We demonstrate successful magnetothermal activation of three separate brain regions, motor cortex, dorsal striatum and the ridge between dorsal and ventral striatum.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing behavioral responses from stimulation in each region.

claim: All three brain regions have been previously activated either optogenetically or chemogenetically.
source: All three have been previously activated either optogenetically (Gradinaru et al., 2007; Kravitz et al., 2010) or chemogenetically (Arenkiel et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The same behavioral responses were observed as had been reported resulting from optogenetic or chemogenetic neurostimulation in those areas.
source: We observed the same behavioral responses as had been reported resulting from optogenetic or chemogenetic neurostimulation in those areas.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of the observed behaviors with those reported in cited prior work.

claim: Successful neurostimulation in vivo was achieved without raising the overall tissue temperature by binding MNPs to the neuronal membrane.
source: We were able to achieve successful neurostimulation in vivo without raising the overall tissue temperature by binding MNPs to the neuronal membrane.
evidence: This is supported by temperature measurements showing localized heating at the membrane without bulk tissue heating.

claim: Exchange-coupled core-shell MNPs combining soft and hard magnetic materials permit independent optimization of the MNP's size and magnetic properties.
source: Exchange-coupled core-shell MNPs combining soft and hard magnetic materials (Cobalt Oxide and Manganese oxide) in a core-shell geometry, permit independent optimization of the MNP's size and magnetic properties (Lee et al., 2011; Zhang et al., 2015b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work on core-shell nanoparticle design.

claim: The synthesized MNPs have an 8.0 ± 1.0 nm Co-ferrite core surrounded by a 2.25 nm Mn-ferrite shell.
source: We synthesized MNPs with an 8.0 ± 1.0 nm Co-ferrite core surrounded by a 2.25 nm Mn-ferrite shell.
evidence: This is a description of the synthesized materials.

claim: The PMA coating added 5.4 ± 1.4 nm to the MNP diameter.
source: The PMA coating added 5.4 ± 1.4 nm to the MNP diameter (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by TEM measurements shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The MNPs used in this study have an SLP of 733.3 ± 2.8 W/g at 37.0 kA/m and 412.5 kHz.
source: The MNPs used in this study have an SLP of 733.3 ± 2.8 W/g at 37.0 kA/m and 412.5 kHz, close to the theoretical maximum for particles of this size (Zhang et al., 2015a).
evidence: This is experimental measurement data.

claim: The fluorescence intensity of DyLight 550 decreased by 2.2% per degree temperature rise.
source: We found that the fluorescence intensity of DyLight 550 decreased by 2.2% per degree temperature rise (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is calibration data shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: To open a sufficient number of TPRV1 channels to affect neuronal firing, the cell surface temperature needs to rise only a few degrees above the physiological temperature.
source: To open a sufficient number of TPRV1 channels to affect neuronal firing, the cell surface temperature needs to rise only a few degrees above the physiological temperature (Huang et al., 2010; Chen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: In the MNP suspension sample, the entire bath temperature rose by two degrees during a seven second AMF heating.
source: In the MNP suspension sample, the entire bath temperature (along with the cells) rose by two degrees (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Following a seven second AMF heating, the MNP suspension required more than 1 min to cool back to the initial temperature.
source: Following a seven second AMF heating, the MNP suspension required more than 1 min to cool back to the initial temperature.
evidence: This is observed from the experimental data in Figure 2C.

claim: When the MNPs were bound to the cell membrane, only the membrane, and not the bath, was heated by several degrees.
source: Conversely, when the MNPs were bound to the cell membrane, only the membrane, and not the bath, was heated by several degrees (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: After removing the AMF, the membrane temperature returned to the initial value within a few seconds.
source: After removing the AMF, the membrane temperature returned to the initial value within a few seconds.
evidence: This is observed from the experimental data in Figure 2D.

claim: For membrane-bound MNPs, the heating rates were 0.1 to 1.0°C/s, depending on the area density of MNP.
source: For membrane-bound MNPs, the rates were 0.1 to 1.0°C/s, depending on the area density of MNP (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The heating power per MNP is 2.55 ± 0.94 fW/particle.
source: Hence, the heating power per MNP is 2.55 ± 0.94 fW/particle, consistent with the prediction from magnetic measurements, 3.34 fW/particle (Zhang et al., 2015a).
evidence: This is calculated from experimental data and compared to theoretical predictions.

claim: From 32°C to 36°C, the Calcium spiking rate was temperature independent.
source: From 32°C to 36°C, the Calcium spiking rate was temperature independent.
evidence: This is observed from experimental data in Figure 3A.

claim: As bath temperature was increased from 37˚C to 39˚C, spontaneous activity of TRPV1+ neurons increased from 1.5 ± 1.2 action potentials per 5 s to 13 ± 3 APs in the same period.
source: As bath temperature was increased from 37˚C to 39˚C, spontaneous activity of TRPV1+ neurons increased from 1.5 ± 1.2 action potentials (APs) per 5 s to 13 ± 3 APs in the same period.
evidence: This is experimental data from calcium imaging experiments.

claim: At 39°C, only about 15–20% of rat TRPV1 channels open.
source: At 39°C, only about 15–20% of rat TRPV1 channels open (Grandl et al., 2010)
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: TRPV1 has an about 1,000-fold higher single channel conductance than ChR2.
source: but the resulting Calcium influx is sufficient to trigger neuronal activity because TRPV1 has an about 1,000-fold higher single channel conductance than ChR2 (Lórenz-Fonfría and Heberle, 2014; Studer and McNaughton, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: In control neurons, without TRPV1, there was a slight decrease of the spiking rate, to 1 ± 1 APs per 5 s at elevated temperatures.
source: In control neurons, without TRPV1, we observed a slight decrease of the spiking rate, to 1 ± 1 APs per 5 s (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Expressing TRPV1 in hippocampal neurons renders their firing rate highly heat-sensitive without disrupting natural function.
source: Therefore, expressing of TRPV1 in hippocampal neurons renders their firing rate highly heat-sensitive without disrupting natural function.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing temperature-dependent firing in TRPV1+ neurons and normal calcium transient shapes.

claim: The spiking frequency increased from 1.8 ± 0.6 per 5 s before AMF to 4.5 ± 1.2 per 5 s during the AMF (n = 13, p=0.0028).
source: The spiking frequency increased from 1.8 ± 0.6 per 5 s, before AMF (field 0 to 5 s), to 4.5 ± 1.2 per 5 s, during the AMF (n = 13, **p=0.0028, unpaired T-test)
evidence: This is experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: The spiking frequency increased to 12.1 ± 2.0 per 5 s immediately following the AMF (n = 13, p=0.0002).
source: and 12.1 ± 2.0 per 5 s immediately following the AMF (n = 13, ***p=0.0002, unpaired T-test, 95% confidence intervals [1.5,2.23] and [10.8,13.3])
evidence: This is experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: 87% of neurons spike during the first 5 s of field application.
source: 87% of neurons spike during the first 5 s of field application
evidence: This is calculated from experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: 64% of the neurons fire already within 2 to 3 s after the field is turned on.
source: and 64% of the neurons fire already within 2 to 3 s after the field is turned on (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is calculated from experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: A histogram of the latencies of all cells exposed to 5-s field stimulation was fitted with a Poisson distribution giving an expectation value of 2.18 ± 0.17 s.
source: A histogram of the latencies of all cells exposed to 5-s field stimulation was fitted with a Poisson distribution giving an expectation value of 2.18 ± 0.17 s (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Robust magnetothermal genetic stimulation requires uniform, sustained over-expression of TRPV1 in the targeted neurons.
source: While some expression of TRPV1 in the rodent brain has been reported (Basbaum et al., 2009), robust magnetothermal genetic stimulation requires uniform, sustained over-expression of TRPV1 in the targeted neurons.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental design requiring viral delivery of TRPV1.

claim: All 6 mice in a total of 14 trials began running along the periphery of the observation arena during AMF application.
source: All 6 mice in a total of 14 trials began running along the periphery of the observation arena (AMF was 7.5 kA/m and 570 kHz; Figure 4A,B, Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is experimental behavioral data.

claim: The linear running speed of the mouse increased from 5.3 ± 2.75 mm/s to 83.8 ± 3.75 mm/s during AMF application (one mouse, four trials, p=5.9·10−6).
source: The linear running speed of the mouse increased from 5.3 ± 2.75 mm/s to 83.8 ± 3.75 mm/s (Figure 4E; one mouse, four trials, p=5.9·10−6, 95% C.I. [0.9, 9.7] and [77.8, 89.8] mm/s).
evidence: This is experimental behavioral tracking data with statistical analysis.

claim: The angular speed increased from 0.21 ± 0.19 rev/min to 3.27 ± 0.30 rev/min during AMF application (p=0.0003).
source: The angular speed increased from 0.21 ± 0.19 rev/min to 3.27 ± 0.30 rev/min (Figure 4F; p=0.0003).
evidence: This is experimental behavioral tracking data with statistical analysis.

claim: Over all 14 trials in 6 mice, the angular speed was significantly faster during AMF applications, 2.81 ± 0.20 rev/min, as compared to 0.34 ± 0.08 rev/min during the rest periods between the fields (p=5.2·10−9).
source: Over all 14 trials in 6 mice, the angular speed was significantly faster during AMF applications, 2.81 ± 0.20 rev/min, as compared to 0.34 ± 0.08 rev/min during the rest periods between the fields (Figure 4G; p=5.2·10−9; 95% C.I. [0.29, 0.39] and [2.69, 2.93] rev/min).
evidence: This is experimental behavioral tracking data with statistical analysis.

claim: For an AMF strength of 7.5 kA/m rms at 570 kHz, the behavioral response began 22.8 ± 2.6 s after the beginning of the AMF (n = 14, 6 mice).
source: For an AMF strength of 7.5 kA/m rms at 570 kHz, the behavioral response began 22.8 ± 2.6 s (n = 14, 6 mice, Figure 4H) after the beginning of the AMF.
evidence: This is experimental behavioral data.

claim: After the AMF is terminated, the ambulation behavior continued for 14.7 ± 2.5 s.
source: After the AMF is terminated, the ambulation behavior continued for 14.7 ± 2.5 s, likely the time required to cool the membrane-bound MNPs (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is experimental behavioral data.

claim: Mice injected with only AAV5-hSyn-TRPV1 virus or only MNPs showed no response to AMF application.
source: Mice injected with only AAV5-hSyn-TRPV1 virus or only MNPs showed no response to AMF application (Videos 3 and 4 respectively)
evidence: This is control experimental data.

claim: Observable stimulation occurred only when AMF was applied in the presence of the temperature-gated ion channel, TRPV1, and the energy transducing MNPs in the same brain locations.
source: Observable stimulation occurred only when AMF was applied in the presence of the temperature-gated ion channel, TRPV1, and the energy transducing MNPs in the same brain locations.
evidence: This is demonstrated by control experiments showing no response without both components.

claim: In all mice injected with both MNP and TRPV1 at the same brain location, angular speed increased significantly with AMF, 3.17 ± 0.17 rev/min compared to the baseline speed of 0.42 ± 0.07 rev/min (n = 10, p=1.1·10−5).
source: On the other hand, in all mice injected with both MNP and TRPV1 at the same brain location, angular speed increased significantly with AMF, 3.17 ± 0.17 rev/min compared to the baseline speed of 0.42 ± 0.07 rev/min (n = 10, p=1.1·10−5; unpaired T-test; 95% C.I. [0.32, 0.52] and [2.94, 3.40] rev/min) (Figure 4I).
evidence: This is experimental behavioral data with statistical analysis.

claim: Membrane targeting the MNPs is essential as animals injected with virus and MNPs without the anti-A2B5 antibody were insensitive to the AMF application.
source: Membrane targeting the MNPs is essential as animals injected with virus and MNPs without the anti-A2B5 antibody were insensitive to the AMF application (Figure 4I, Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is control experimental data.

claim: Chemogenetic activation of the caudate putamen nuclei in the striatum has previously been shown to evoke increased locomotion in the form of rotation around the body axis.
source: Chemogenetic activation of the caudate putamen nuclei in the striatum has previously been shown to evoke increased locomotion in the form of rotation around the body axis (Arenkiel et al., 2008; Kreitzer and Malenka, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: During AMF application, the mouse turns around its body axis, so that its head tracks circles of 22 ± 5 mm radius.
source: During AMF application, the mouse turns around its body axis, so that its head tracks circles of 22 ± 5 mm radius (Figure 5A-C, Video 3).
evidence: This is experimental behavioral tracking data.

claim: These turns were very regular and quick (19.3 ± 2.2 mm/s), resulting in 4.7 ± 0.8 revolutions per minute.
source: These turns were very regular and quick (19.3 ± 2.2 mm/s; Figure 5D), resulting in 4.7 ± 0.8 revolutions per minute (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is experimental behavioral tracking data.

claim: The mice turned contralateral to the injection in 11 out of 12 trials.
source: The mice turned contralateral to the injection in 11 out of 12 trials and did never reverse the direction of turning after initiating the motion.
evidence: This is experimental behavioral observation.

claim: The average response of four striatum targeted mice in 12 trials was a 6-fold increase in angular speed during AMF activation, 2.86 ± 0.19 rev/min compared to a baseline rate of 0.47 ± 0.09 rev/min (p=3.4·10−7).
source: The average response of four striatum targeted mice in 12 trials was a 6-fold increase in angular speed during AMF activation, 2.86 ± 0.19 rev/min compared to a baseline rate of 0.47 ± 0.09 rev/min (Figure 5G; p=3.4·10−7; unpaired T-test; 95% C.I. [0.42, 0.56] and [2.71, 3.01] rev/min).
evidence: This is experimental behavioral data with statistical analysis.

claim: The observed response is consistent with a prior report of dorsal striatum stimulation by capsaicin activation of TRPV1 channels at the same brain coordinates.
source: The observed response is consistent with a prior report of dorsal striatum stimulation by capsaicin activation of TRPV1 channels at the same brain coordinates (Arenkiel et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The Deisseroth team showed that optogenetic stimulation near the ridge between dorsal and ventral striatum inhibits voluntary locomotion.
source: The Deisseroth team showed that optogenetic stimulation near the ridge between dorsal and ventral striatum inhibits voluntary locomotion (Gradinaru et al., 2009; Kravitz et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Application of AMF caused freezing of gait (FOG), characterized by the inhibition of locomotion, with all four paws locked in place while the mouse was still able to move its head in all directions, neck onward.
source: Application of AMF caused freezing of gait (FOG), characterized by the inhibition of locomotion, with all four paws locked in place while the mouse was still able to move its head in all directions, neck onward.
evidence: This is experimental behavioral observation.

claim: FOG is common in patients with advanced Parkinson disease.
source: FOG is common in patients with advanced Parkinson disease (Moore et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior clinical work.

claim: During AMF application, the average linear speed decreased significantly, from 17.7 ± 2.2 mm/s before stimulation to essentially rest, 1.04 ± 0.13 mm/s (two mice, six trials; p=0.0006).
source: During AMF application, the average linear speed decreased significantly, from 17.7 ± 2.2 mm/s before stimulation to essentially rest, 1.04 ± 0.13 mm/s (Figure 6C; two mice, six trials; p=0.0006; unpaired T-test; 95% C.I. [15.4, 20.1] and [0.90, 1.18] mm/s).
evidence: This is experimental behavioral data with statistical analysis.

claim: The tracked speed during the AMF was indistinguishable from that of a fixed marker on the arena floor (0.52 ± 0.11 mm/s).
source: The tracked speed during the AMF was indistinguishable from that of a fixed marker on the arena floor (0.52 ± 0.11 mm/s).
evidence: This is experimental control data.

claim: Magnetothermal genetic stimulation leads rapidly to the targeted motor behavior, observable within 15–20 s of AMF activation.
source: Magnetothermal genetic stimulation leads rapidly to the targeted motor behavior, observable within 15–20 s of AMF activation.
evidence: This is observed from the behavioral experiments.

claim: This brief delay is not an intrinsic limit of the technique, but rather the result of a weak average field at the site of the mouse head.
source: This brief delay is not an intrinsic limit of the technique, but rather the result of a weak average field at the site of the mouse head (Figure 4—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is inferred from the field strength measurements and comparison to in vitro results.

claim: As the heating rate is proportional to the square of magnetic field strength, the threefold weaker field caused approximately nine times longer latency in the mouse than observed in the in vitro studies.
source: As the heating rate is proportional to the square of magnetic field strength, the threefold weaker field caused approximately nine times longer latency in the mouse than observed in the in vitro studies.
evidence: This is inferred from theoretical understanding and comparison of in vitro and in vivo results.

claim: The evoked locomotor behavior diminished quickly within 15 s after removal of the field.
source: Likewise, our results show that the evoked locomotor behavior diminished quickly within 15 s after removal of the field.
evidence: This is observed from the behavioral experiments.

claim: Three to four one-minute stimulations were possible within a 10–15 min experiment.
source: In our experiments, three to four one-minute stimulations were possible within a 10–15 min experiment.
evidence: This is observed from the experimental protocol.

claim: MNPs were bound via the A2B5 antibody, which indiscriminately recognizes all glycosylated membrane proteins.
source: In this study, MNPs were bound via the A2B5 antibody, which indiscriminately recognizes all glycosylated membrane proteins.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental method.

claim: The A2B5 antibody yielded the highest nanoparticle density on the cell surface and accordingly, achieved the most rapid heating.
source: It yielded the highest nanoparticle density on the cell surface and accordingly, achieved the most rapid heating.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison of different antibody targeting approaches.

claim: Anti-CD56 (Thy-1), anti-CD90 (NCAM) for endogenous membrane proteins, as well as anti-GFP to target overexpressing GFP-labeled membrane proteins were also successfully used.
source: However, we also successfully used anti-CD56 (Thy-1), anti-CD90 (NCAM) for endogenous membrane proteins, as well as anti-GFP to target overexpressing GFP-labeled membrane proteins.
evidence: This is a description of alternative experimental approaches tested.

claim: The antibody binding limits the distance that the MNP diffuse into the brain.
source: The stimulation region is spatially better confined as the antibody binding limits the distance that the MNP diffuse into the brain (Figure 5—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is supported by histological data showing MNP spread.

claim: Only cell types with the specific membrane receptor targeted by the antibody bind the nanoparticles.
source: Also, only cell types with the specific membrane receptor targeted by the antibody bind the nanoparticles (Figure 5—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is supported by histological data showing cell-specific MNP binding.

claim: Robust activation was obtained with as little as 500 ng of nanoparticles, which is 200-fold lower than the volume of nanoparticle suspension for brain neuron stimulation in anesthetized mice.
source: Lastly, we obtained robust activation with as little as 500 ng of nanoparticles, which is 200-fold lower than the volume of nanoparticle suspension for of brain neuron stimulation in anesthetized mice (Chen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a comparison to prior work, supported by citation.

claim: Stimulation of the same animals was successfully repeated for seven to eight trials over a few days without observing any change in normal or evoked behavior.
source: We successfully repeated stimulation of the same animals for seven to eight trials over a few days without observing any change in normal or evoked behavior.
evidence: This is experimental observation.

claim: Histology of brains after 20 one-min AMF applications, spread over three sessions during a 24 hr period, showed intact MNP decorated neurons.
source: Also, histology of brains after 20 one-min AMF applications, spread over three sessions during a 24 hr period, showed intact MNP decorated neurons (Figure 5—figure supplement 7).
evidence: This is histological data.

claim: Several animals could share the stimulation arena simultaneously, and only animals injected with MNPs would be affected by the AMF.
source: For instance, several animals could share the stimulation arena simultaneously, and only animals injected with MNPs would be affected by the AMF.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about potential applications.

claim: Adapting the field geometry allows controlling the stimulation timing and condition.
source: Hence, adapting the field geometry allows controlling the stimulation timing and condition.
